topics.title: Therapeutic, Nonverbal & Assertive Communication
topics.summary: Use clear words, read nonverbal cues in context, reply in ways that help the client talk, and speak up assertively for safety.
objectives: You can explain verbal, nonverbal, written, and electronic communication.
You can pick a therapeutic reply and spot a communication barrier.
You can read a nonverbal cue in context instead of guessing its meaning.
You can tell passive, aggressive, and assertive messages apart.
You can match the channel to how urgent and private a message is.
You can check that a message was truly understood.
topics.bigPicture:
Communication is how people share information and feelings. It should lead to a response, such as a safer choice, a reported symptom, or a skill the client can do. Saying the words is not enough. A message works only when the other person understands it.

Words, tone, posture, face, silence, and timing all send messages. Therapeutic communication is purposeful talk that serves the client’s needs. Assertive communication lets you state a safety concern clearly without attacking anyone. You will use both skills every shift, and the NCLEX tests them often.
recap: Words and body language should match. When they do not, gently explore the mismatch.
A nonverbal cue is data to clarify, not proof of what someone feels or intends.
Open questions, reflection, empathy, clarification, and silence invite the client to say more.
False reassurance, advice, judgment, changing the subject, and defensiveness block communication.
Assertive means direct, honest, and respectful: state the finding and the action you need.
If a safety concern is brushed off, restate it clearly and use the escalation pathway.
Urgent symptoms need direct, immediate contact, not a routine portal message or email.
A nod or “I understand” is not proof. Ask the client to explain or show you.

keyTerms.def: Sharing a message with words, either spoken or written.
Messages sent without words, such as facial expression, gestures, posture, movement, appearance, and touch.
When words, tone, and body language all agree. Incongruence means they send different messages.
Purposeful, professional talk that helps the client express needs, feel understood, and take part in care.
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no. It invites the client to explain in their own words.
Restating the feeling or main idea the client shared so they can confirm or explain more.
Promising an outcome the nurse cannot guarantee, such as “Everything will be fine.” It shuts down the conversation.
Stating your needs, concerns, and requests directly and honestly while respecting the other person’s rights.
The receiver’s response. It shows whether the message was understood as intended.
The sender gives a message, the receiver repeats it back, and the sender confirms it is correct.

sections.heading: What makes a message clear?
sections.keyIdea: A message succeeds only when the other person understands it and can act on it.
sections.source: Communication slides 3–4, 10
sections.body:
Communication is any way two or more people exchange information or feelings. All communication aims to get a response. Its two main purposes are to influence others to respond and to obtain information.

Your slides cover verbal, nonverbal, electronic, and written communication. Written communication counts as a form of verbal communication.

The course lists seven things to consider when you speak. Use them as a quick checklist.

A correct lecture can still fail. A client in pain may not take in a single word. Watch the response and adjust. Never guess an answer to sound credible. Say you will check, and then follow up.
bullets: Pace and intonation: how fast you speak and your tone change how the message feels and its impact.
Simplicity: use commonly understood words. Explain any medical term you must use.
Clarity and brevity: be direct and simple. Your words and body language should match (be congruent).
Timing and relevance: choose a moment when the client can listen, and keep to what matters now.
Adaptability: adjust to the client’s behavior.
Credibility: be honest, consistent, and dependable.
Humor: can reduce stress and tension. Use it only when it fits, because it can make distress seem small.

sections.heading: How do I read nonverbal cues?
sections.keyIdea: Nonverbal cues can say more than words. Read each cue in context, and ask instead of assuming.
sections.source: Communication slides 5–7, 12, 28
sections.body:
Nonverbal communication includes gestures, facial expressions, touch, body position and movement, and physical appearance. It can express more about feelings than words do. It can support the words or contradict them.

Assess it in a systematic way. Include mental status, gestures and facial expressions, and posture and gait.

No single expression can be read accurately by itself. Consider other cues that back it up, the setting, the expressions of others there, and cultural background.

When words and nonverbal cues do not match, the course says to believe the nonverbal message. Describe what you see and ask about it. Do not accuse the client of lying.
sections.example: A client says, “I’m fine,” but grimaces and guards the belly when moving. The nurse says, “You say you are comfortable, and I notice you are guarding your belly. Tell me what you are feeling.” The nurse explores before deciding anything.
bullets: Ask before you touch, and explain why the touch is needed.
Respect personal space. Sit at a comfortable distance with a relaxed, open posture.
If a client flinches or crosses their arms, consider pain, fear, or past trauma.
Chart the behavior you saw, not a label like “hostile” or “uncooperative.”

headers: What it can mean (per the course)
rows: Happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, or disgust. Confirm with other cues and the setting.
Can be affected by money or by illness. Ill clients may lack the energy or desire to engage. Disinterest in hygiene may indicate depression.
Show self-concept, current mood, and health. Erect posture and an active, purposeful stride suggest well-being.
May come from changes in cognition, autism, or intellectual disability.

sections.heading: Which replies are therapeutic?
sections.keyIdea: Therapeutic replies invite the client to share meaning. Pick the technique that fits your purpose right now.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (Communication slide 14 names therapeutic techniques but does not list them)
sections.body:
Your slides point to videos on therapeutic techniques but do not list them. This table gives the standard techniques the NCLEX expects. Each technique has a job. No single technique is always correct. Choose the one that fits what you need in this moment.

Open questions let the client describe a concern in their own words. A focused closed question gets one fact fast.

If you need the time chest pain started, ask, “What time did the pain start?” That focused question is the right tool there.

Silence is a technique, too. After hard news, quiet presence gives the client time to feel and think. Listening means following the client’s meaning, not waiting for your turn to talk.

rows: Reflection. Names the feeling and invites detail.
“You sound worn out by all of this.”
Sit with the client quietly and stay attentive.
Focused question. Gets a time-critical fact.

check.q: Is a closed question ever the best choice?
check.a: Yes. When you need a time-critical fact, such as when chest pain started, a focused closed question fits the purpose.

sections.heading: Which replies block communication?
sections.keyIdea: Barriers shut the conversation down, so the nurse never learns what the client actually needs.
sections.source: Communication slide 13; “why” questions added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
A barrier is a reply that stops the client from sharing. Many barriers sound kind or efficient. They still close the door, so you never learn what the client needs.

Your course lists eleven barriers (below). Note that agreeing is on the list, along with disagreeing. Both judge the client’s view as right or wrong. Instead, acknowledge the feeling and explore it.

“Why” questions are not on the course list, but the NCLEX treats them as barriers. “Why did you do that?” can sound like blame. “What was happening when that occurred?” invites the story.
bullets: Stereotyping: assuming meaning from a group the client belongs to.
Agreeing and disagreeing: “You’re right” or “That’s wrong.” Both judge the client’s view.
Being defensive: protecting yourself, other staff, or the facility instead of hearing the concern.
Challenging: making the client prove a statement or point of view.
Probing: asking for details mainly out of curiosity, not to help the client.
Testing: asking questions that make the client admit to something.
Rejecting: refusing to discuss certain topics with the client.
Changing topics and subjects: “Let’s talk about lunch.” It avoids the concern.
Unwarranted or false reassurance: “Don’t worry, it will be fine.” It promises what you cannot guarantee.
Passing judgment: approving or disapproving. Clients stop sharing.
Giving common advice: “If I were you, I would…” It replaces the client’s values with yours.

sections.heading: Passive, aggressive, or assertive?
sections.keyIdea: Assertive communication is direct, honest, and appropriate. It stands up for the nurse or client while respecting others.
sections.source: Communication slides 15–16
sections.body:
Your course describes three types of communicators (table). The assertive style is the most productive.

Assertive communicators use “I” statements rather than “you” statements: “I am concerned about this new change, and I need you to assess the client now.” Assertive does not mean louder. It means standing up for yourself, or your client, while staying open to other ideas.

rows: Focuses on the needs of others. Tries to meet their requests. Often denies own power or authority.
“Sorry to bother you. I’ll call back if anything changes.” The safety concern stays unaddressed.
Focuses on own needs and becomes impatient when they are not met. Asserts own rights without considering others. May seem self-righteous or superior. Often felt as a personal attack.
“You always say that.” Or: “Fine, I’ll report you.”
Declares and affirms opinions. Respects others’ right to speak assertively, too. Communicates directly, honestly, and appropriately.
“I understand you’re busy. This is a new change. I need you to assess the client now.”

sections.heading: What does an assertive nurse do?
sections.keyIdea: Assertive nurses stay calm, use “I” statements, and repeat a clear request. The course names specific techniques to practice.
sections.source: Communication slides 17–19; escalation note added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
An assertive nurse is professional and advocates for the client. Ideas are expressed directly and without confrontation. The approach is nonjudgmental and non-blaming, which makes a win-win result more likely.

The course names nine techniques (below). Agreeing with part of a criticism never means dropping a safety issue. If the concern stays unresolved, use your facility’s escalation pathway.

rows: Freedom to express self. Awareness of own rights. Self-control over strong emotions. Open to other points of view. Relaxed body language and a well-modulated tone. Able to receive feedback.
Improves communication and outcomes. Reduces stress. De-escalates conflict. Reduces the chance of angry encounters.

bullets: “I” statements: “I am concerned…” instead of “You never…”
Fogging: find even a small area of agreement and build from there. “I understand the unit is busy.”
Negative assertion: agree with valid criticism without anger, then focus on the positive.
Repetition: calmly restate one clear message: the finding and what you need.
Confidence.
Managing nonverbal communication: calm voice, relaxed and open posture.
Thinking before speaking.
Avoiding apologizing whenever possible.
Post-conversation evaluation: afterward, ask whether your concern was specific and your request clear.

sections.heading: Which channel fits the message?
sections.keyIdea: Match the channel to urgency and privacy. Urgent, abnormal, or highly confidential information should not go electronically.
sections.source: Communication slides 8–10
sections.body:
Electronic tools include client portals, email, social networks, and text messaging. They improve access, but they add risks. Confidentiality can be breached. Clients who cannot afford text messaging will not get appointment reminders.

Your course gives the rules below for electronic messages.

Written communication is a form of verbal communication. It makes context hard to show. Effective writing uses appropriate terms, correct grammar and spelling, logical order, and proper citation of sources.
sections.example: A clinic nurse reads a portal message sent 10 minutes ago. Since starting a new blood pressure pill, the client’s lips and tongue are swelling, and swallowing is getting hard. This is time-sensitive. The nurse contacts the client directly right away and follows the emergency protocol. A routine portal reply is not enough.
bullets: Do not use electronic channels when: information is urgent, diagnostic findings are abnormal, or the information is highly confidential.
Get consent: clients should agree to email contact.
Label it: state in the subject line that the email is confidential. The label alone does not secure it, so also use the approved secure system.
Remember: email can be used in court.
Do not replace talk: electronic messages are not a substitute for effective in-person communication. Use professional judgment.

sections.heading: How do I know the message worked?
sections.keyIdea: Feedback shows understanding. Ask the client to explain in their own words or show you.
sections.source: Communication slides 3, 29, 35; Ex D slides 3, 6
sections.body:
All communication aims to get a response. Feedback is the receiver’s response. Your course says to evaluate feedback to confirm that communication is working.

A nod is not enough. It may mean politeness, uncertainty, or confusion. Ask the client to explain the plan in their own words or demonstrate a skill. If something is missing, clarify without blaming them.

With the team, close the loop on critical messages. The receiver repeats the request, timing, and follow-up, and the sender confirms. Then document the key details and the client’s response.
sections.example: A client starting a new anticoagulant (blood thinner) says, “Yes, I understand.” Stronger evidence is the client explaining, in their own words, what to watch for and what to do. Agreement alone does not show learning.
bullets: The client communicates needs effectively, and the needs are met.
The client demonstrates a skill, such as correct inhaler use.
The client expresses less frustration, fear, or anxiety.
The client uses available resources appropriately.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers sound kind but promise, advise, judge, back down, or avoid the real concern.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — review of Communication slides 5–19, 28–35
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Empathy names the feeling: “You sound scared.” False reassurance promises an outcome: “It will be fine.”
Assertive targets the problem and the request. Aggressive targets the person or makes threats.
Passive apologizes and backs off. Assertive restates the finding and the need now.
“What happened?” invites the story. “Why did you…?” can sound like blame.
Silence is attentive presence. Avoidance is leaving or changing the subject.
Acknowledge the feeling. Agreeing and disagreeing are both course barriers, because they judge the client’s view.
Describe and ask: “I notice…” Do not decide the cue means lying or anger.
Agreement is not evidence. Explanation in the client’s own words or a demonstration is.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the reply that keeps the client talking, fits the purpose, and protects safety.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Communication items often ask for the “most therapeutic” reply. Others ask what to do first when cues do not match. Select-all items may ask which replies are barriers.

Sample question: A client says, “I don’t think I can handle chemotherapy again.” Which reply is most therapeutic?

A: “Don’t worry, this round will be easier.”
B: “If I were you, I would finish the treatment.”
C: “What part feels hardest to face this time?”
D: “Let’s talk about your lunch order.”
bullets: “Most therapeutic reply”: look for an open question, reflection, or empathy about the client’s own words.
Mismatched cues: explore gently before acting on the words alone.
Barrier select-all items: false reassurance, advice, and changing the subject.
Provider pushback: choose the calm, specific, direct request, not the apology or the threat.
Channel questions: urgent symptoms need direct, immediate contact.
steps: Read the stem: the client voices doubt and fear about more treatment.
What is it really asking? Which reply helps the client share the concern?
Key cues: “I don’t think I can” hints at a hidden worry. It could be fear, side effects, or practical problems.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A is false reassurance. B is advice that replaces the client’s values. D changes the subject.
The answer: C. An open question invites the client to explain what feels hardest.
Strategy: Cross out any option that promises, advises, judges, or changes the subject. Then pick the reply that focuses on the client’s feelings.

sections.heading: Worked case: “I suppose I will manage”
sections.keyIdea: Uncertain words plus quiet cues are a reason to explore, not to reassure.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Communication slides 5–7, 13, 29, 35
sections.body:
A client is being discharged with new equipment. The client says, “I suppose I will manage,” then stares at the equipment and goes quiet.

The nurse could say, “You will do fine.” But that would not reveal the real worry.

The concern could be fear, understanding, physical ability, cost, or support. Only exploring will show which one it is.
steps: Notice the cues: hesitant words, a long look at the equipment, sudden silence.
Ask a neutral open question: “What part of managing at home feels uncertain?” Then wait.
Listen. The client says, “I know the steps, but I can’t reach the supplies.”
Match the action to the need: assess function and adapt the setup. Another lecture would not help.
If the client fears being a burden, acknowledge it and ask what support they want. Do not force family involvement.
If a language or hearing barrier exists, fix access before you judge the response.
Verify: ask the client to explain or show the plan. Then ask if the worry has been addressed.

check.q: Why is “You will do fine” weaker than exploring here?
check.a: It promises a result without finding the real barrier. The need might be equipment, practice, resources, or emotional support.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 38 Communication slides 1–35
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 38 slides.
bullets: Module 38 Communication, slides 2–19 (process, forms, barriers, communicator types) and slide 28 (believe nonverbal cues when they conflict with words).
Feedback and evaluation: slides 29 and 35. Closed loop and read-back: Ex D slides 3 and 6.
Not in the slides: the therapeutic-technique table and “why” questions. They come from standard NCLEX content.
Clarification: the course says to mark an email as confidential in the subject line. Do this, but the label is not a security control. Also use the approved secure system.

pearls: Nonverbal cues invite assessment. They do not prove intent.
Empathy acknowledges feelings without promising outcomes.
Assertive replies are specific, direct, and respectful. They name the finding and the action needed.
If two replies both seem kind, choose the one that invites the client to say more.
Match the channel to urgency, and verify understanding through feedback.
redFlags: Urgent deterioration needs immediate, direct communication and escalation, not a message that may be read later.
A message sent through an unapproved channel can expose confidential information.
A provider brushing off a new unsafe finding requires respectful persistence and the escalation pathway.

checks.q: A client says “fine” while grimacing. What is a therapeutic response?
checks.a: Gently describe what you notice and ask about discomfort. Do not accuse the client of being inconsistent.

checks.q: How is assertiveness different from aggression?
checks.a: Assertiveness states a concern and request directly while respecting the other person. Aggression attacks, threatens, or ignores the other person’s rights.

checks.q: Does labeling an email “confidential” secure it?
checks.a: No. The course says to mark the subject line confidential, but you must also use the approved secure system and verify the recipient.

checks.q: Why is nodding not enough evidence of understanding?
checks.a: A nod may reflect politeness, uncertainty, or confusion. Ask the client to explain in their own words or demonstrate.

checks.q: A client sits quietly with tears after hearing a cancer diagnosis. What should the nurse do first?
checks.a: Stay with the client and use attentive silence. Give time before asking questions or offering information.

topics.title: Communication Across the Lifespan & With Impairment
topics.summary: Find the real communication barrier, protect the client’s own voice, and choose practical supports you can test and document.
objectives: You can assess understanding, expression, senses, language, and thinking as separate barriers.
You can adapt communication to a client’s developmental level and preferences.
You can use qualified interpreters and communication aids correctly.
You can avoid elderspeak, stereotypes, and assumptions about competence.
You can write and evaluate a functional communication goal.
You can recognize a new communication problem as a possible emergency.
topics.bigPicture:
A communication barrier is a mismatch between what the client needs and the method you are using. Shouting at someone with aphasia does not help. Neither does small print for someone with poor vision, or repeating English to someone who needs another language.

Start by assessing how the person takes in and expresses information. Then change the setting, timing, language, device, or support. Keep talking to the client directly. Being unable to speak does not mean being unable to understand, decide, or take part.
recap: Assess understanding (receptive) and expression (expressive) separately. One can work when the other does not.
Fix sensory access first: hearing aids in, glasses on, noise down, then judge understanding.
Use a qualified interpreter for clinical information. Avoid using children or family as routine interpreters.
Speak to the client directly, even when family or an interpreter helps.
Avoid elderspeak like “sweetie” or “good girl.” Age alone does not mean reduced ability.
Offer adolescents private time and explain the limits of confidentiality honestly.
Write functional goals, and judge them by accurate use, not by an aid being nearby.
Sudden aphasia or new weakness is an emergency. Get urgent help while supporting communication.

keyTerms.def: Taking in and understanding a message, whether spoken, written, or shown.
Getting a message out through speech, writing, gestures, or another method.
A language problem caused by brain injury, such as a stroke. It can affect speaking, understanding, reading, or writing.
Trouble getting words out. The person may understand well but struggle to speak or name objects.
A tool that helps a person understand or express needs, such as a picture board, writing pad, or tablet.
Talking down to an older adult with baby talk, pet names, or exaggerated praise. It harms dignity.
A trained person who can interpret medical information accurately and impartially in person, by phone, or by video.
A goal that names a real task the client will do, such as using a board to report pain.

sections.heading: How do I find the real barrier?
sections.keyIdea: Find out exactly which part of communication is blocked before you choose a fix.
sections.source: Communication slides 29, 33
sections.body:
Start by evaluating the client’s communication style. Look for any language or communication barriers. Keep cultural values and practices in mind. Assess the ability to communicate both verbally and nonverbally.

Separate sensory access from language and thinking. A client may understand perfectly once hearing aids are in. Ask what has helped before.

Keep evaluating feedback to confirm that communication is working. Once you find a method that works, note it in the EHR and make the aid available. Do not keep testing the client through a channel that fails.
bullets: A hearing aid, medical alert bracelet, or similar item.
The client trying to read your lips.
The client trying to use their hands to sign.
sections.example: An older adult keeps asking the nurse to repeat instructions. The hearing aids are in a bedside drawer, and the TV is loud. First, help the client put in the hearing aids and turn down the TV. Then check understanding.

sections.heading: What speech and thinking changes should I note?
sections.keyIdea: Cognitive problems, some medicines, and conditions like delirium can change speech and understanding. Describe exactly what you hear.
sections.source: Communication slides 30–32
sections.body:
Disorders that impair thinking can affect the ability to use and understand language. Some medicines can impair speech, too. A client may lose the ability to find or name words, have impaired articulation, or lose speech completely.

Cognitive impairment, psychosis, delirium, or severe depression can alter thought processes. Signs include repeating the same words or phrases, talking about people or things that are not present, and flight of ideas.

Use the table to assess both verbal and nonverbal communication.

rows: Does the client speak fluently or hesitate? Use words correctly? Follow directions? Repeat words or phrases when asked?
Slow or rapid, spontaneous or hesitant, quiet or overly loud, aggressive, or evasive.
Any change from normal. Acute illness or extreme distress may cause words the client would not normally use.
Trouble with a specific sound, lack of clarity, trouble speaking in sentences, loose associations, or flight of ideas.

check.q: A client who usually answers clearly now talks about people who are not in the room. What should the nurse note?
check.a: An altered thought process. Describe the exact behavior. Because it is a change, assess for causes such as delirium and report it.

sections.heading: Which fix fits which barrier?
sections.keyIdea: Each barrier needs its own adaptation and its own way to check that it worked.
sections.source: Communication slides 27, 34
sections.body:
Your course names four ways to improve communication (below). Then use the table to match the method to the barrier.

Every row ends with a check. An adaptation only counts if the client can actually use it.

rows: Face the client, reduce noise, check that hearing aids work.
Can the client restate the message accurately?
Offer paper and pencil, a communication board, a tablet, or pictures, as appropriate.
Can the client reliably communicate a need?
Use large print, good lighting, and spoken description.
Can the client use the information?
Does the client show understanding through the interpreted exchange?

check.q: A client with low vision but normal hearing needs discharge teaching. What helps?
check.a: Read key points aloud, use large print and good lighting, and ask the client to explain the plan back. Adapt to the actual barrier, which is vision.

bullets: Manipulate the environment: control noise level and lighting.
Provide support: encouragement and nonverbal reassurance.
Enhance communication: use words with simple, concrete meanings, and stay on topic.
Avoid cultural barriers: watch your gestures, use interpreters, and understand cultural norms.

sections.heading: How do I talk with children and teens?
sections.keyIdea: Match the message to the child’s development, include the child directly, and build rapport with teens without judgment.
sections.source: Communication slides 21–24; teen confidentiality example added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Infants communicate nonverbally. They perceive through their senses. Watch for two kinds of cues: engagement (ready to interact) and disengagement (needs a break). Learn each infant’s expressive messages.

Toddlers are gaining expressive and receptive language. Let them finish their thoughts without interrupting. Give simple answers and one-step directions, because attention spans are short.

School-age children need chances to express themselves. Adolescents can think abstractly and make decisions about their own health care. They feel a strong need to share thoughts and feelings, but building rapport takes time.

Assess each child as an individual.

rows: Learn the infant’s engagement and disengagement cues. Respond calmly and consistently.
Assuming no speech means no message.
Time to finish without interruption. Simple answers. One-step directions. Drawings, pictures, and photos.
Interrupting. Long explanations or multi-step directions.

Eye level. Include the child in the talk and in care. Listen openly. Answer honestly in words they understand. Stories, drawing, painting, or other art. Books or movies about a similar condition. Writing for older children.
Saying “it won’t hurt.” Talking only to adults.
Active listening. A nonjudgmental attitude and nonreactive behavior. Clearly explained expectations. Praise.
Showing judgment or shock. Teens are very sensitive to feeling judged.

sections.example: A 15-year-old comes for a sports physical with a parent. The nurse needs to ask about sexual activity and substance use. First, the nurse arranges private time with the teen and explains confidentiality and its limits. Some information, such as risk of serious harm, may need to be shared.

sections.heading: What about adults, pregnancy, and family?
sections.keyIdea: Adults vary widely, so look for barriers. In pregnancy, learn the family’s birth values and share decisions with the client.
sections.source: Communication slides 25–26
sections.body:
Young and middle-aged adults are at the peak of their communication abilities. Still, abilities vary widely. Young adults may keep some adolescent patterns. In upper middle age, some begin to have the physical or cognitive problems seen in older adults. Identify any barriers and plan for them.

During pregnancy and birth, therapeutic communication is essential to safety and comfort. Find out the family’s cultural values about birth. Engage in shared decision making. Listen to the client as well as give support.

Speak to the pregnant client directly. Do not assume a partner speaks for her. Not everyone in a culture shares the same values.
sections.example: During labor, a partner says, “I make the decisions. In our culture, she agrees with whatever I say.” The nurse asks the client privately about her decision and support preferences. The nurse speaks to her directly and includes the partner as she wishes. The nurse neither stereotypes nor dismisses the culture.

sections.heading: How do I talk with older adults?
sections.keyIdea: Remove sensory and cognitive barriers, speak simply without talking down, and believe nonverbal cues when words disagree.
sections.source: Communication slides 27–28
sections.body:
Older adults may have sensory deficits, cognitive impairment, neurologic deficits, or psychosocial problems that affect communication. Make sure glasses and hearing aids are in and working. Offer aids such as paper and pencil, a communication board, a tablet, or pictures. Refer to services and resources as needed.

Elderspeak means baby talk, pet names, or exaggerated praise. It harms dignity. Short, simple sentences are not elderspeak. Speaking only to family when the client can take part also harms dignity.

New language trouble or confusion may need urgent assessment, not just a new strategy.
sections.example: A nursing assistant tells an alert 82-year-old, “Good girl, sweetie! Let’s take our pills now.” The nurse addresses this with the assistant and models adult-to-adult speech, using the client’s preferred name.
bullets: Keep environmental distractions to a minimum.
Speak in short, simple sentences.
Avoid elderspeak.
Always face the client when speaking.
Include family and friends in the conversation.
Believe the nonverbal message when it conflicts with the words.
Pay careful attention to the client’s feelings.
Find out what is important to the client, and try to maintain it.

sections.heading: How do I use interpreters and aids?
sections.keyIdea: A qualified interpreter or a tested aid carries the client’s own voice. Neither replaces it.
sections.source: Communication slides 27, 33–34; interpreter details added from current practice standards
sections.body:
Your course lists interpreters as a way to avoid cultural barriers. Current practice standards add detail. Use a qualified medical interpreter by phone, video, or in person, per policy.

Family may give emotional support. They should not replace qualified interpretation for clinical information. Avoid using children as interpreters. A translated handout can support an interpreted session. It cannot replace one.

For aids, help the client get access to any assistive device. Note it in the EHR and keep it available. Choose based on vision, movement, literacy, and comprehension. Placing a board within reach does not prove it works.

Practice with the client. Refer to services such as speech-language pathology when needed.
bullets: Speak directly to the client, not to the interpreter.
Talk in short segments, and pause for interpretation.
Allow questions.
Verify understanding through the interpreted exchange, such as teach-back.
sections.example: A client who speaks Vietnamese and limited English needs teaching for a new insulin regimen. The client’s 12-year-old offers to interpret. The nurse arranges a qualified medical interpreter by phone, video, or in person instead.

sections.heading: How do I plan and evaluate communication care?
sections.keyIdea: Set a functional goal, judge it by real use, and escalate any new communication loss urgently.
sections.source: Communication slides 33–35; sudden-aphasia point added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Use the nursing process (ADPIE: assess, diagnose, plan, implement, evaluate). The course diagnosis is difficulty with communication. It may be receptive (understanding) or expressive (getting a message out).

Plan with the client. Course goals: the client will have an effective method of communicating, and will maximize the ability to understand and be understood. Make goals functional: “By end of shift, the client will use the board to communicate pain, toileting, and position needs.”

Evaluate with the course outcomes (below). Put the working method in the EHR and handoff.

Do not equate slow speech with low competence. Sudden aphasia, new weakness, or a drop in alertness needs emergency evaluation per protocol. Any one alone is enough.
steps: Assess understanding and expression separately.
Identify sensory, language, thinking, movement, and environment needs.
Choose the method together with the client.
Practice and verify that messages come through accurately.
Document the method, the help needed, and the client’s response.
bullets: The client communicates needs effectively, and the needs are met.
The client demonstrates a skill, such as correct inhaler use.
The client expresses less frustration, fear, or anxiety.
The client uses available resources appropriately.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers usually judge ability too fast, hand the client’s voice to someone else, or miss an emergency.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — review of Communication slides 20–35
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Expressive aphasia blocks words out. The client may still understand and decide.
Fix hearing aids and noise first. Then judge understanding.
Family can comfort. A qualified interpreter handles clinical information.
Board within reach vs. board that works
The goal is met when the client uses it accurately for real needs.
Assess function. Avoid elderspeak. Short, simple sentences are a course strategy, but never talk down.
Offer teens privacy, but explain the limits of confidentiality.
A long-standing aphasia needs adaptation. Sudden aphasia needs emergency evaluation.
Ask the client directly and privately about her preferences.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Choose the answer that removes the real barrier and keeps the client at the center of the conversation.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Questions often describe an older adult, a child, a language need, or aphasia. The right answer usually fixes access first or protects the client’s voice. Watch for sudden neurologic change hidden in the stem.

Sample question: A client who spoke normally earlier suddenly cannot get words out and has new arm weakness. What should the nurse do first?

A: Give the client a picture board.
B: Ask family how the client usually communicates.
C: Get urgent evaluation per stroke or rapid response protocol.
D: Document expressive aphasia in the care plan.
bullets: “What should the nurse do first?” with hearing aids in a drawer: fix sensory access.
Child offers to interpret: choose a qualified interpreter.
Family answers for the client: speak to the client directly and allow time.
Goal evaluation: pick the finding showing accurate, functional use.
Teen visit: private time plus honest limits of confidentiality.
steps: Read the stem: speech was normal earlier. Now it is suddenly gone, with new arm weakness.
What is it really asking? Is this a communication problem or a medical emergency?
Key cues: “suddenly” and “new arm weakness” point to an acute neurologic event.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and B support communication but delay emergency care. D only records the problem.
The answer: C. A new communication deficit may be a clinical emergency.
Strategy: Ask, “Is this new?” A new change from baseline is assessed and escalated before you adapt.

sections.heading: Worked case: protect the client’s voice
sections.keyIdea: Slow down, use a tested method, and let the client answer for themselves.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Communication slides 29–34
sections.body:
A client had a stroke 2 years ago and has long-standing expressive aphasia. During admission, staff ask questions quickly, and the client becomes frustrated.

The spouse begins answering every question. Yet the client follows one-step directions and points accurately to pictures.

These cues show the client understands and can express needs another way. A communication disability does not mean the client cannot decide. The spouse’s speed should not decide who takes part.
steps: Slow down. Reduce distractions and ask one question at a time.
Offer a picture board or another method that fits the client’s vision, movement, literacy, and energy.
Verify that yes and no and other choices are reliable.
Speak directly to the client. Kindly explain to the spouse why waiting for an answer matters.
Set a functional goal, such as reporting pain and position needs with the board.
Document the method and help needed, and name it in handoff.
Because this aphasia is long-standing, adapt. If it were new, get urgent evaluation first.

check.q: What is the best evidence that the board is working?
check.a: The client accurately communicates real needs, such as pain or toileting, using it. Having the board nearby or pointing once is not enough.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 38 Communication slides 20–35
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 38 slides.
bullets: Module 38 Communication, slides 20–28 (lifespan) and 29–35 (nursing process).
Added from current practice standards: qualified interpreters, not using children to interpret, teen confidentiality limits, and treating sudden aphasia as an emergency.
Course strategy for older adults: short, simple sentences. This is not elderspeak, which the course says to avoid.

pearls: Assess expression and understanding separately.
A communication aid must be usable and tested with the client.
Address the client directly, even when family or an interpreter helps.
Age or limited speech does not mean the client cannot decide.
When a stem says “suddenly,” think emergency before adaptation.
redFlags: Sudden aphasia or new one-sided weakness needs urgent evaluation.
A new inability to communicate essential needs creates immediate pain and safety risks.
Using a child to interpret clinical teaching risks errors and burdens the child.

checks.q: A client with aphasia follows instructions but cannot name objects. What should be assessed separately?
checks.a: Understanding and expression. Offer another way to communicate while you continue to assess.

checks.q: What is an appropriate direction for a toddler?
checks.a: One short, concrete step at a time, with time to respond.

checks.q: How should the nurse speak during an interpreted encounter?
checks.a: Speak directly to the client in short segments, allow questions, and verify understanding through the qualified interpreter.

checks.q: Is a communication board enough when aphasia suddenly begins?
checks.a: No. Support communication, but get urgent assessment for the acute neurologic change.

checks.q: An 8-year-old needs an IV. What approach fits?
checks.a: Explain honestly at eye level in concrete words, let the child see or handle supplies, and invite questions. Do not say it won’t hurt.

topics.title: Documentation: Accurate Records, Privacy & Continuity
topics.summary: Record what you assessed, did, communicated, and saw afterward, using factual, timely, and secure documentation.
objectives: You can explain the clinical and legal purposes of the health record.
You can write objective notes that separate what you saw from what others reported.
You can correct errors and make late entries without falsifying the record.
You can compare common charting systems, including charting by exception.
You can protect record privacy and secure your workstation.
You can document teaching, discharge, and referral needs clearly.
topics.bigPicture:
The health record lets the whole team share one accurate picture of the client. It supports care planning, continuity, quality review, education, payment, and legal accountability. A good note tells a clear care story. Another nurse should be able to read it and know what happened and what is still needed.

Charting never comes before safety. If a client gets worse, assess, act, and escalate first. Then document promptly and accurately. The note should show what really happened, in the real order, with the client’s response.
recap: If a client deteriorates, act and escalate first. Document promptly afterward.
Never chart care before it happens. Precharting creates a false record.
Describe behavior and quote the client. Avoid labels like “difficult” or “noncompliant.”
Attribute reports to their source. Do not chart findings you did not verify.
Correct errors through the approved process. Never erase, hide, or backdate.
Charting by exception still requires defined standards and required flow sheets.
Log off when you are not using the computer, and use only your own login.
A family relationship alone does not authorize disclosure. Verify the caller and the client’s wishes.

keyTerms.def: Specific findings you can see, hear, measure, or feel, written without judgment or guessing.
What the client reports feeling or experiencing. Mark it as the client’s report, and quote key words.
Documenting care before it is done. It is never acceptable because plans change.
An addition made after the event. It is clearly labeled and shows both the entry time and event time, per policy.
The electronic record of who opened, entered, or changed information and when. It supports accountability.
A system that documents changes from defined normal standards. It depends on clear norms and required flow sheets.
A standard plan listing the expected outcomes and care for a clinical course, often day by day.
An unexpected event or response that changes the planned course on a critical pathway.
A HIPAA rule to limit health information shared to what is needed. It does not apply to sharing among providers for treatment.

sections.heading: Why does the record matter?
sections.keyIdea: The record is the shared care story that keeps the next clinician safe and accurate.
sections.source: Ex C slides 3, 6, 16
sections.body:
Each client record is a formal, legal document. The Joint Commission and other accrediting agencies require it. Follow your organization’s own policies for documenting and reporting.

The course lists eight purposes of the record (below). Each depends on notes that are accurate, timely, and complete.

Documentation never replaces direct communication. If you notice a client getting worse while charting, stop. Assess, act, and escalate first. Then document the change and show the follow-up actions you took.
bullets: Communication among team members and across shifts.
Planning client care.
Auditing health agencies.
Research.
Education.
Reimbursement, which means payment for care.
Legal documentation of the care given.
Health care analysis.
sections.example: While charting, a nurse notices the client’s oxygen saturation is 86% on room air and the client is newly confused. The nurse stops charting, acts on the low oxygen, and escalates. Documentation comes promptly afterward.

sections.heading: What goes into a good note?
sections.keyIdea: A good note meets legal standards and shows the finding, the action, who was told, and what happened next.
sections.source: Ex C slides 15–16
sections.body:
Besides keeping records confidential, nurses must meet legal standards for documenting. The course lists what every entry needs (below).

Before charting, read prior notes. Document any change in condition and show that follow-up actions were taken. “Provider aware” is incomplete. The reader needs what was reported, when, to whom, the reply, and what happened next.

Be mindful of abbreviations. Use only approved ones, because an unclear one can change the meaning. Do not carry forward an assessment you did not perform. Before you finish, review the note for clarity and accuracy.

rows: Describe the relevant symptoms, function, and findings.
Record the decision, the stated reason, teaching given, and follow-up.
Include the time, clinician, findings reported, response, and plan.
Include the content, learner, method, response, and remaining needs.

bullets: Date and time.
Accepted terminology.
Correct spelling.
Signature, if on paper.
Accuracy.
Sequence: events in the order they happened.
Appropriateness.
Completeness.
Conciseness.

sections.heading: How do I chart facts, not labels?
sections.keyIdea: Describe what you saw and heard, quote the client, and name the source of every report.
sections.source: Ex C slide 16
sections.body:
Your course says to use objective, specific, factual descriptions. Do not use vague terms or record assumptions.

Describe behavior instead of labels. “Client shouted, ‘Leave me alone,’ and turned away during care” tells more than “client difficult.”

Record the client’s actual words in quotation marks. A quote keeps the meaning, though it does not prove every claim in it. Document the client’s response to each intervention.

Separate your own assessment from another person’s report. Never document for someone else.
sections.example: A transfer note says, “Ambulates independently.” The daughter says the client usually walks alone at home. The nurse has not seen the client walk. Accurate entry: “Daughter reports client walks independently at home. Gait not yet assessed by this nurse.”

sections.heading: How do I fix errors and late entries?
sections.keyIdea: Never chart in advance or alter a record. Correct errors by following agency policy.
sections.source: Ex C slides 5, 16; late-entry details added from current practice
sections.body:
Never document in advance of an event. A planned medicine or assessment may be delayed, refused, or changed. Charting early creates a false record. Be timely: chart as soon as you can after care, while keeping safety first.

Never alter a record. Know your agency’s policy for correcting an entry error, and follow it. Keep the original entry and the audit trail visible. Do not erase, hide, backdate, or quietly overwrite.

Late entries are not on the slides. In current practice, a late entry shows both when it was written and when the event happened, per policy.
sections.example: At 1030, a student’s note says, “1200 medication given, tolerated well.” The nurse must intervene. That medication has not been given yet.

sections.heading: How do I protect privacy?
sections.keyIdea: Keep all client information confidential, open only records tied to your role, and log off when you step away.
sections.source: Ex C slides 4–5; family-disclosure and minimum-necessary notes added from current HIPAA guidance
sections.body:
The ANA Code of Ethics says the nurse has a duty to keep all client information confidential. Follow agency policies for record privacy. Access is limited to health care professionals involved in that client’s care. HIPAA sets rules for the privacy, confidentiality, and security of protected health information.

Students may access records for education, research, client studies, conferences, clinical rotations, and rounds. Use access only for those purposes. Curiosity about a neighbor or a public figure is never one.

A family relationship does not automatically allow disclosure. Privacy rules have specific exceptions, so neither “always share” nor “never share” is right. HIPAA’s minimum-necessary rule does not apply to sharing with providers for treatment.
bullets: Log off the computer when you are not actively using it.
Make sure information is not visible to others while in use.
Know the agency’s policy for correcting an entry error.
Follow agency policies for documenting sensitive material.
Use only your own login. Never chart under a colleague’s session.
sections.example: A caller says, “I’m the client’s sister. How did her surgery go?” The nurse first verifies the caller per policy, such as with a client code. The nurse then checks the client’s documented wishes about sharing.

sections.heading: Which charting systems will I see?
sections.keyIdea: Systems differ in format, but each must tell the same accurate care story.
sections.source: Ex C slides 7–11
sections.body:
Your course names six documentation systems (table). Whatever the system, the record must tell the same accurate care story.

Charting by exception (CBE) records significant or unexpected findings, or exceptions to defined norms. It has three key elements: flow sheets, standards of nursing care, and bedside access to records. It does not mean “chart nothing.”

Critical pathways are part of case management. They stress quality, cost-effective care with a multidisciplinary approach. A pathway names the outcomes a certain group of clients should reach each day of care, and the interventions needed each day.

A variance is an unexpected response that affects the plan of care. Document the unexpected event and the interventions used in response.

rows: Organizes the record around the client’s problems.
Centers on a client concern. A common format is Data, Action, Response (not on the slides).
Records significant or unexpected findings, measured against defined standards.
Uses standardized lists, drop-down menus, and nurse narrative. Easy to retrieve within and across agencies. eMARs track medicines, speed prescribing, and use audit tracking to help limit errors.
Day-by-day expected outcomes and interventions. Unexpected events are charted as variances.

check.q: A new nurse says, “With charting by exception, I don’t chart routine care.” Is this right?
check.a: No. CBE writes out only exceptions to defined norms. It depends on standards of nursing care and flow sheets, where routine care is still recorded.

bullets: Pathway advantages: promotes collaboration and reduces length of stay.
Pathways work best for clients with only one or two diagnoses and few individualized needs.
A client with an unpredictable course can be hard to document on a pathway.

sections.heading: What records follow the client’s stay?
sections.keyIdea: The admission assessment sets the baseline. Care plans, flow sheets, and progress notes track the client from there.
sections.source: Ex C slides 12–13
sections.body:
The admission assessment is a comprehensive assessment done when the client is admitted to the unit. It may be called the initial assessment. Its purpose is to evaluate the client’s health status and identify functional health problems.

After that, three kinds of records track care (table). Keep them current as findings and priorities change.

rows: Assessments, nursing diagnoses or care priorities, nursing interventions, and client outcomes. It is evidence of the current plan of care.
Graphic record (such as vital signs), intake and output (I&O) record, and medication administration record (MAR).
Client progress, problems or expectations, nursing interventions, and evaluations of those interventions.

sections.heading: What about teaching, discharge, and transfer?
sections.keyIdea: Document all teaching. Discharge and transfer records must show current status and every ongoing need.
sections.source: Ex C slides 14, 16
sections.body:
Document all teaching. Name the learner, content, method, and response. Include teach-back or demonstration results, barriers, and next steps. A printed packet does not prove understanding.

Discharge instructions given to the client or family must be in understandable terms.

If the client transfers within the facility or to a long-term care facility, a report goes with the client for continuity of care. It includes all parts of the discharge instructions. It also describes the client’s condition before transfer and any teaching done.

A referral should include the items below.
bullets: Physical, cognitive, and mental health status at discharge.
Continuing health problems and current care needs.
Treatments to be continued.
Current medication list.
Restrictions on moving, diet, and bathing.
Education and instruction given at discharge.
sections.example: “Reviewed inhaler steps with client using demonstration. Client correctly performed four steps, omitted exhalation before use, then completed the full sequence after reteaching. Written plan provided; follow-up practice scheduled.”

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers chart first, chart early, chart labels, or hide mistakes.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — review of Ex C slides 4–16
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: If the client is getting worse, act and escalate first. Chart afterward.
Chart only care that has happened. Never prechart.
“Shouted and pushed the washcloth away” is a description. “Hostile” is a label.
“Daughter reports” differs from what you assessed yourself.
Corrections keep the original and audit trail. Erasing or backdating hides them.
CBE writes out exceptions to defined norms. Routine care is still recorded on flow sheets.
Name who, when, what was reported, the reply, and the plan.
Verify identity and the client’s wishes before sharing.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Pick the entry that is factual, timed, attributed, and honest about what was and was not done.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect “which entry is best” and “which entry needs follow-up” items. Select-all items often list confidentiality actions or referral content. Priority items test whether you act before charting.

Sample question: During morning care, a client shouts at the nurse and pushes a washcloth away. After pain medicine, the client accepts care 30 minutes later. Which entry is best?

A: “Client hostile and uncooperative.”
B: “Client shouted ‘Leave me alone’ and pushed washcloth away. Reported pain 7/10. Pain medicine given per order. 30 min later, accepted care.”
C: “Client refused care due to bad attitude.”
D: “Client was upset but is fine now.”
steps: Read the stem: a behavior, a likely cause, an action, and a later response.
What is it really asking? Which entry is objective and tells the full care story?
Key cues: shouting, a timed intervention, and a changed response 30 minutes later.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A and C use labels and guess at motives. D is vague and has no findings or times.
The answer: B. It quotes the client, names the action, and shows the timed response.
Strategy: Choose the entry a stranger could act on: facts, quotes, sources, times, and outcomes.

sections.heading: Worked case: complete the care story
sections.keyIdea: Connect the concern, the action, and the response so the next nurse knows what is still needed.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Ex C slide 16
sections.body:
At 1030, a client declines a dressing change and says, “I am afraid it will hurt.” The nurse assesses pain, discusses options, and gives the ordered pain medicine. At 1100, the client reports less pain and agrees to care.

“Pain addressed; provider aware” would not tell the next nurse anything useful. A clear note connects the events instead of calling the client difficult.
steps: Record the client’s concern as a quote, with pain findings and time.
Document the actual intervention with the real time it was given.
Record the reassessment and the client’s response at 1100.
Do not chart the later agreement before it happens.
If the client still declined, chart the informed choice, the stated reason, actions, and notification.
Name any unresolved needs and follow-up clearly.

check.q: Why is “teaching done, understands” an incomplete care story, too?
check.a: It names an action and a conclusion but not the content, method, learner response, remaining gaps, or how understanding was checked.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.source: Module 38 Ex C slides 1–16
sections.body: This lesson follows your Module 38 Exemplar C slides.
bullets: Module 38 Ex C, slides 2–16.
Privacy clarification: HHS minimum necessary guidance (hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/minimum-necessary-requirement); checked October 27, 2026.
The minimum-necessary rule has an exception for disclosures to, or requests by, healthcare providers for treatment.
Added from current practice: late-entry rules, the Data, Action, Response format for focus charting, and family-disclosure rules.
Local documentation and access policies decide the exact steps, such as EHR correction buttons and deadlines.

pearls: Document actual care and the client’s response. Never prechart.
Objective wording describes behavior, not motive.
Correct errors openly through the approved process.
Charting by exception depends on defined standards.
When an exposed record is found, secure it first, then follow reporting policy.
redFlags: Acute deterioration needs direct assessment and escalation. Charting alone is not enough.
Looking at unrelated records, sharing logins, or unsecured disclosure can breach confidentiality.
A copied or precharted finding may falsely represent care that never happened.

checks.q: What is wrong with documenting a medication before it is given?
checks.a: It may not be given as planned, so the entry creates a false record of care.

checks.q: Does charting by exception eliminate routine records?
checks.a: No. It relies on clear standards and required flow sheets.

checks.q: What is a pathway variance?
checks.a: An unexpected event or response that changes the planned course. Document it, the actions taken, and the response.

checks.q: How should an error in a finalized EHR entry be corrected?
checks.a: Use the approved correction process. Keep the original and the audit trail. Do not hide or backdate.

checks.q: A workstation shows a client record open under a colleague’s login. What first?
checks.a: Lock or secure the screen. Do not enter anything under that login. Then follow policy for reminding or reporting.

topics.title: Reporting, Handoff, SBAR & Telephone Orders
topics.summary: Pass on a clear current picture, name what is still unresolved, and close the loop on every request, result, and order.
objectives: You can describe handoff as a transfer of information, authority, and responsibility, with time for questions.
You can organize a focused SBAR report with a clear request.
You can prepare for a provider call without delaying emergency care.
You can receive telephone results and orders safely, using read-back.
You can follow up and escalate when a concern is not resolved.
topics.bigPicture:
Reporting turns your assessment into team action. At every handoff, the next clinician needs to know who the client is, what changed, what is being done, and what is still unresolved. A long history with no priorities helps less than a short, organized report.

Good handoff is a conversation, not a list read aloud. The receiver asks questions and confirms. You stay responsible for spotting urgency, making a clear request, and following up if the client is still not safe.
recap: A handoff transfers information, authority, and responsibility. Allow questions, and name pending tasks and who owns them.
SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The Recommendation is your specific request.
Unstable client? Call for urgent help first. Do not delay to perfect a report.
Before a routine call, have the client’s name and diagnosis, changes in findings and vitals, pertinent labs, related interventions, and your request ready.
Never guess a missing value. Say you do not know and verify it.
Telephone orders and critical results: write it down, read it back, and get confirmation.
Read-back checks the words. It does not prove the order is safe.
If the client worsens after your report, reassess and escalate again.

keyTerms.def: A verbal or written transfer of information, authority, and responsibility during a care transition, with a chance to ask questions, clarify, and confirm.
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. A structure for a short, focused clinical report.
Repeating a written-down order or result to the sender so they can confirm it is correct.
A message is sent, repeated back, and confirmed, so both people share the same planned action.
A result, task, reassessment, or decision that is still unfinished at handoff.
Getting the next level of help when a concern is urgent or unresolved, such as a rapid response team.
A test value that may be dangerous and needs prompt reporting and action, such as potassium 6.6 mEq/L.
An order given by phone or spoken aloud. Who may give or take one depends on the Board of Nursing, scope, and facility policy.

sections.heading: What makes a handoff useful?
sections.keyIdea: A handoff transfers information, authority, and responsibility, and gives the receiver a chance to ask, clarify, and confirm.
sections.source: Ex D slides 3–4
sections.body:
A handoff is a verbal or written transfer of information, authority, and responsibility during a transition of care. It covers all nursing care given and all team members who cared for the client during that time.

Every handoff includes a chance to ask questions, clarify, and confirm. A written report sent without that chance does not complete it.

Identify the client with the required identifiers. Select information that changes what the next nurse understands or does. If a test is pending, say it is pending. Do not imply it was normal.
bullets: Current status and any significant changes.
Relevant treatments, recent tests or procedures, and new orders.
Risks, safety needs, and priorities.
What needs reassessment, when, and who is responsible.
sections.example: “Repeat assessment is due at 1900, and the ordered test result is pending. Please review it with the clinician.” This helps far more than “tests done.”

sections.heading: What are the four parts of SBAR?
sections.keyIdea: SBAR moves from what is happening now to exactly what you need next.
sections.source: Ex D slide 5
sections.body:
SBAR was developed by the U.S. Navy as a framework for safe, efficient communication between team members. It reduces miscommunication during handoffs, transfers, and shift changes. It helps improve client safety and team satisfaction.

Background is information relevant to the situation, not the full history. Assessment is your analysis and the options you see, within your role.

Never leave the Recommendation blank. You may not write medical orders, but you can recommend a bedside assessment, a clarification, a treatment review, or help. Make the urgency clear.

rows: A concise statement of the problem.
New inattention and drowsiness began this afternoon.
Postoperative day one. Normally alert and independent.
Your analysis and consideration of options.
“Vital signs are stable, but this is a new change in thinking. It could be a medicine effect or early delirium.”
A recommendation based on the relevant information.
“I am requesting that you assess the client at the bedside now.”

check.q: During an SBAR call, the nurse says, “Respiratory rate is 28 and oxygen saturation is 89%. I think fluid may be building up in the lungs.” Which SBAR part is this?
check.a: Assessment. The nurse analyzes the findings and considers what may be happening. The Recommendation follows with a specific request.

sections.heading: How do I prepare for a call?
sections.keyIdea: Prepare well for a stable client, but never let preparation delay help for an unstable one.
sections.source: Ex D slide 6; urgent-response point added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
Assess the client first. Know your specific concern and request. This prevents vague calls like “the client seems off.”

Match preparation to urgency. If the client is unstable, activate the urgent response pathway and stay with the client. Give a short report when help arrives.

Your course says to be concise and accurate. Have the chart ready, and make the report with the client’s record open. If you do not know a fact, say so and check. Never invent a number. Confirm the plan before you hang up.
bullets: Course list: the client’s name and medical diagnosis.
Course list: significant changes in your assessment and vital signs.
Course list: pertinent lab data.
Course list: related nursing interventions.
Also helpful: current medications, allergies, and a specific request.
Not needed: every past surgery from every admission.
sections.example: A nurse is gathering labs for an SBAR call about rising drowsiness. Back in the room, the client responds only to pain and breathes 8 times a minute. The nurse activates the rapid response team and stays with the client.

sections.heading: What goes in shift and transfer reports?
sections.keyIdea: Report what changed, what works, and what is still pending, not every unchanged detail.
sections.source: Ex D slide 4; Ex C slide 14
sections.body:
A change-of-shift report follows a specific order and is concise. Your course lists what it covers (below).

Also cover safety needs, assistance, communication methods, monitoring, and pending follow-up. For a client with delirium, report the baseline, the change, how it fluctuates, and what calms the client. Protect privacy at the bedside, involve the client when appropriate, and invite questions.

Transfer reports go with the client. They include current condition, ongoing needs, medicines and treatments, restrictions, and teaching. Verify key details rather than trusting the old record.
bullets: Essential identifying information.
Reason for admission and current status.
Diagnostic tests or interventions in the past 24 hours.
Significant changes in condition and newly started HCP orders.
A clear statement of the priorities of care.

sections.heading: How do I receive a phone result?
sections.keyIdea: Document it, repeat it back, then notify the provider directly and assess the client.
sections.source: Ex D slide 6; critical-result example added for the NCLEX
sections.body:
When someone calls with a report, document the date, time, caller’s name, and subject of the information. Repeat the information back to the caller to confirm you understood. Critical results need prompt, direct action.

A voicemail or routine electronic message may not meet the requirement for urgent notification. When you report, confirm who will act and when. Writing “notified” does not show the concern was understood.
sections.example: The lab calls with a critical potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. First, the nurse records the result and the caller’s name and reads the value back. Then the nurse promptly notifies the provider directly and assesses the client. Potassium this high can cause dangerous heart rhythms.

sections.heading: How do I take a telephone order?
sections.keyIdea: Capture the whole order, clarify anything unclear, read it back, and get confirmation before acting.
sections.source: Ex D slides 7–8
sections.body:
Facilities may have their own policies. Many allow only RNs to receive telephone orders. Know your Board of Nursing’s (BON’s) position on who can give and accept verbal and phone orders. Wider use of EHRs has reduced telephone orders.

Names, numbers, units, and frequencies are easy to mishear. Read-back checks that you heard correctly. It does not prove the order is safe. Question any drug, dose, or change that does not seem right for the client.

The provider countersigns the order within the time set by facility policy.
steps: Know the BON’s position, and follow the facility’s policy and procedure.
Ask the HCP to spell any medication name you do not know.
Question any drug, dose, or change that does not seem appropriate for the client.
Write down or enter the complete order in the EHR, per facility policy.
Read it back to the HCP. Use words instead of abbreviations. Have the HCP confirm the read-back. “Okay, got it” is not a read-back.
Transcribe the order with the date and time received. Indicate it was a telephone order.
Sign your name and credentials as required.
Follow protocol so the HCP signs or verifies the order within the required time.
Follow facility protocols and best practices for entering dosages.

check.q: A drug name on a phone order sounds unfamiliar, and the dose seems off. What first?
check.a: Ask the prescriber to spell the drug and clarify the dose. Do not pick the closest familiar name or silently “fix” the order.

sections.heading: What if the client worsens after reporting?
sections.keyIdea: Communication does not finish care. Reassess, and escalate again if the response does not match the risk.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
After a handoff or urgent call, check that the receiver knows the top priority, open tasks, and plan if the client worsens. Did the expected response happen? Is the client changing?

If help is delayed or the client gets worse, reassess and escalate through the proper pathway. Document reports, orders, clarifications, actions, and outcomes with exact times.
sections.example: A nurse used SBAR to report a blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg and asked for bedside evaluation. The provider said to recheck in 4 hours. Thirty minutes later, the heart rate is 124/min and the client is restless. The nurse reassesses and escalates now.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers delay help for a perfect report, guess at unclear details, or assume one call ends the job.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — review of Ex D slides 3–8
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many missed questions. Learn how to tell them apart.

rows: Background is context. Recommendation is the action you need next.
Situation is a concise statement of the problem. Assessment is your analysis and the options you see.
Stable client: gather data. Unstable client: get help now.
Read-back confirms the words. Judgment decides if the order is safe.
“Everything is in the chart” vs. handoff
A handoff names priorities, pending items, and owners out loud.
Critical findings need direct, prompt, acknowledged communication.
If the client worsens after the call, escalate again.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Choose the option that matches urgency, makes a clear request, and closes the loop.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials
sections.body:
Expect “what should the nurse do first” items about deteriorating clients. Others ask which statement completes SBAR. Select-all items test telephone-order steps and handoff safety.

Sample question: A nurse reported a client’s new inattention, postoperative history, current vitals, and focused findings. Which statement best completes the SBAR?

A: “The client had surgery yesterday.”
B: “I wanted to let you know.”
C: “I am requesting that you assess the client at the bedside now.”
D: “The client seems confused.”
steps: Read the stem: the nurse already gave Situation, Background, and Assessment.
What is it really asking? Which part is missing? The Recommendation.
Key cues: “best completes” means the final SBAR step.
Why the wrong options are wrong: A repeats Background. B makes no request. D is vague Situation or Assessment.
The answer: C. It is a specific, actionable request.
Strategy: First ask, “Is this client unstable?” If not, pick the answer with a clear request and confirmation.

sections.heading: Worked case: report the next decision
sections.keyIdea: A handoff should hand over the next decision, not just the chart.
sections.source: Added: worked example based on Ex D slides 3–8
sections.body:
Near shift change, a client has a new assessment finding. A repeat check is due at 1900, and a test result is pending.

The outgoing nurse says, “Everything is in the chart.” That does not clearly transfer the open priorities.

If the client is getting worse now, use the urgent pathway. Do not wait for the next shift.
steps: Describe current status and the new concern.
Give relevant background and what has already been done.
Name the pending result, the 1900 reassessment, and who will review them.
State what to do if the client worsens.
Invite questions and confirm the receiver can name the top priority.
If a phone order comes in, write it, clarify, read back, and confirm.
Document the exchange and follow up on any requested help.

check.q: What separates Recommendation from Background in this report?
check.a: Background explains relevant context. Recommendation states the action or response needed next, with urgency when it matters.

sections.source: Module 38 Ex D slides 1–8; Ex C slide 14

Module 38 Ex C, slide 14 (discharge and transfer content).
The Ex D outcomes list the care plan conference, but no slide teaches it.
Added for the NCLEX: escalation when a client worsens after reporting, and the critical-result example.
Who may give or receive verbal orders follows your Board of Nursing, professional scope, and facility policy.

mnemonics.name: SBAR
mnemonics.text: Situation: a concise statement of the problem. Background: relevant information. Assessment: my analysis and the options. Recommendation: what I recommend or need you to do.

pearls: The Recommendation states the requested next action.
A handoff includes unresolved tasks and a chance to ask questions.
Read back the recorded order and get confirmation.
Clarify uncertainty before acting. Never guess a drug name or value.
A critical lab result: record, read back, then notify the provider directly and assess the client.
redFlags: Unstable findings need urgent response without waiting for a perfect report.
An unclear or unsafe order must be clarified before action.
A critical message that no one acknowledged may leave the risk unresolved.
A client who worsens after a “wait and recheck” plan needs prompt re-escalation.

checks.q: Which SBAR part holds the request for a bedside review?
checks.a: Recommendation.

checks.q: What belongs in report when a test result is pending?
checks.a: That it is pending, why it matters, and who will review it and follow up.

checks.q: Does read-back replace judging whether an order is appropriate?
checks.a: No. Clarify incomplete or unsafe orders even if you heard the words correctly.

checks.q: A client has a new change in alertness, but not every lab from last week is gathered. What first?
checks.a: Escalate now with current findings and a clear request. Gather more detail only if it does not delay help.

checks.q: Name three features of a safe bedside handoff.
checks.a: It is focused on priorities, protects privacy, invites questions, and names pending tasks and who owns them.
